title: Mòrag judges the empty salt trade a war in waiting
summary: Mòrag Chruaidh hears the third salt-trader in a summer return empty-handed from the southern shore and judges aloud, in her father's hall, that a household with salt and no king and a household with a king and no salt cannot go on as they are, and resolves to go south herself rather than wait a season for word to reach Dòmhnall in the north.

title: Eleven spears go south by the drovers' track
summary: Mòrag takes eleven men south along the coast track the hill's own herders use to drive beasts to winter grazing, telling them on the road that the raid is to take salt and nothing more: no house burned, no beast lifted beyond a needed ox, no blood shed that the salt-folk do not themselves choose to shed defending it.

title: Donnchadh Bàn falls at the shelters
summary: Donnchadh Bàn, Mòrag's father's oldest belted man, is the first of the seven to fall in the raid on the salt-scrapes at Baile ghorm, cut down at the mouth of the turf shelters as the salt-folk come down onto the shingle.

title: Mòrag turns back once on the strand
summary: With the salt loaded and her people falling back up the strand, Mòrag turns once before full light to look at her seven dead among the stones, and resolves that their names will not be let go the way a lost beast or a broken tool is let go.

title: The seven of the raid named at the hill
summary: At the turn of the winter after the raid, on the night the hill keeps for its dead, Mòrag stands at her father's hearth and names all seven who fell at Baile ghorm aloud, in the order they fell, beginning the naming that the hill goes on keeping at the same fire every year after.

title: The salt-folk raise a bank behind the pans
summary: Within two summers of Mòrag's raid the folk of Baile ghorm raise a bank of shingle and turf behind the tide line and dig shallow clay-lined basins inside it, a means of making salt by sun and wind alone that needs no fire a raider can find burning in the dark.

title: Word of the bank reaches the reciters as an answer
summary: Traders who carry the first news of the clay basins up the valley road to Dùn ìseal understand, and say to each other more freely than they say to Mòrag herself, that the bank behind the shingle was raised as much against the hill's spears as against the sea.

title: The king hears the raid from Mòrag's own mouth
summary: Riding down to Dùn ìseal with a small company, the king hears the whole of the salt raid from Mòrag herself and tells her plainly that the south is not yet his to forbid or to avenge, neither blaming nor praising what she has done.

title: Mòrag rides west to the Red Hill
summary: The king takes Mòrag with him on the long ride west to the Red Hill, saying little of his purpose, so that she comes to the lake shore not knowing why she has been brought, only that she has been brought to see something.

title: Seonag weighs the pebble bag before the king
summary: Seonag nic Uisdein meets the king at her own gate and weighs the worn bag that holds one pebble for every household of the Red Hill's shore, and the king weighs it after her and says he is content, the whole business settled without a word of tribute asked or given.

title: Mòrag rides home weighing a different holding
summary: On the road back east Mòrag turns Seonag's pebble bag over in her mind against her own eleven spears and seven dead, and never again raises a raid, though she never tells anyone plainly that the pebble bag is the reason.

title: Two of the first pots reach Dùn ìseal
summary: A trader carries word of the new coiled clay pots fired at Doire shean up to Dùn ìseal, glad for once to be carrying news rather than salt, and Mòrag has two of the first pots set on her own hearth, where they outlast her holding of the hill.

title: Word of the dug-out at Cidhe Beag reaches the hill
summary: Telling of the oak dug-out sunk and left at the landing at Cidhe Beag, the first boat of its kind hollowed whole rather than built plank by plank, reaches Mòrag by the same slow road that carries most new things to whoever holds Dùn ìseal, though she never sees the boat itself.

title: Iain Dubh takes the hill from Mòrag's hand
summary: Mòrag gives up Dùn ìseal to Iain Dubh, a son of the king older than she is by every reckoning but younger to look at, judging that a holder is ill served by staying past the age when she still has something to learn from the holding.

title: Iain Dubh asks Mòrag how she did it
summary: At the gate on the day he takes the hill, Iain Dubh asks Mòrag the one question no one else in the household has put to her directly, how she went south with eleven spears against a whole shore and came home with only seven lost, and she answers him as plainly as she is able.
